newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya says talks with IMF on aid not collapsed.
newsitem.headline: Kenya says talks with IMF on aid not collapsed.

text.p: Kenyan Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi said on Thursday government talks with the International Monetary Fund on an aid package had not collapsed.

Officials said treasury and IMF officials met in Nairobi until early on Thursday, discussing measures the government plans to introduce to stem graft in Kenya including a statutory authority to fight corruption.
"The talks have not collapsed," Mudavadi told Reuters, adding that he would give more details at a news conference called for 3 p.m. (1200 GMT).
An IMF deadline set last month for the government to take action to show its commitment to fight corruption and reform the energy sector or lose a big IMF package expires on Thursday.
The shilling fell against the dollar and pound because of market uncertainty ahead of the IMF decision.

Forex dealers said the market traded nervously as anxious foreign investors and business managers awaited the make-or-break IMF verdict expected to be announced in Washington later on Thursday or early on Friday.
The shilling weakened to 58.92 to the U.S. dollar, down from Wednesday's 58.06 close.

One dealer played down the importance of the IMF, saying the weakening was symptomatic of political instability in the last few weeks as the opposition tried to corner President Daniel arap Moi on constitutional reforms.
Nine people died in clashes between riot police and pro-reform demonstrators in the Kenyan capital early in July, an incident that severely jolted foreign investors.
The IMF extended a three-year Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) loan worth $205 million in April last year but payments were conditional on Kenya meeting promises on reform.

The last scheduled ESAF payment, $36 million, was delayed by the IMF for a month from June 30, mainly because of concern at how Kenyan authorities had handled the multi-million dollar Goldenberg International financial scandal.
The IMF hit out at the government failure to "take decisive steps to ensure transparency and accountability in the use of public funds and resolve outstanding energy sector reform".
The IMF has quoted Goldenberg International to illustrate just how Kenyan authorities are reluctant to punish corruption.

In 1991 and 1992 the government paid a company called Goldenberg International about $100 million under an export compensation scheme for gold and diamond exports. Kenya produces little gold and has no diamond deposits.
Mudavadi said on Tuesday that the government was drafting a bill to set up an anti-graft authority but he would not give any details on when it will be ready.
Senior Energy Ministry officials also said a bill was being drafted to set up an independent energy regulatory board. Mudavadi said that bill was one of the items on the IMF agenda.
